The roar of a great multitude… like the rushing of many waters and mighty thunder

Ezekiel compares the sound of the cherubim's wings and the voice of God's glory to 'many waters' (Ezekiel 1:24; 43:2); Daniel's heavenly man speaks with a voice like a multitude (Daniel 10:6). Thunder accompanies the Sinai theophany (Exodus 19:16) and the 'voice of the LORD' in Psalm 29.

The same sound attributed to Christ's voice (1:15) and to the 144,000 (14:2) now belongs to the redeemed multitude (7:9). Their praise shares the overwhelming quality of a theophany: the church's worship is caught up into God's own glory.
He has judged the great prostitute… avenged the blood of His servants

The language of avenging the blood of God's servants echoes the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:43) and 2 Kings 9:7, where Jehu is commissioned to avenge the prophets' blood on Jezebel — the archetypal seductive persecutor (Revelation 2:20). Prophetic indictments of cities as harlots include Tyre (Isaiah 23:16-17), Nineveh (Nahum 3:4) and, strikingly, Jerusalem itself (Isaiah 1:21; Ezekiel 16 and 23).
Rome was personified as the goddess Roma, shown seated on seven hills on a coin of Vespasian (AD 71). Imperial wealth and luxury were often satirised by Roman moralists as corruption.
The verdict closes the prostitute vision of chapters 17-18. God's judgments are 'true and just' (16:7); the martyrs' cry 'how long?' (6:10) is answered. The identity of the prostitute is disputed.

Many partial preterists (Chilton, Gentry) identify the prostitute as apostate Jerusalem, guilty of the blood of prophets and apostles (Matthew 23:35-37), judged in AD 70; Revelation 19 then celebrates the end of the old covenant order. Others in the school identify her with Rome.
Classic Protestant historicists (Elliott, Barnes) see papal Rome, the 'mother' of a corrupt Christendom that shed the blood of the saints, whose final overthrow is celebrated here.
Futurists see an end-time world religious-commercial system (often centred on a literal city, sometimes rebuilt Babylon) destroyed in the last days just before Christ's return.
Idealists read the prostitute as the seductive world system of every age — economic, cultic and political idolatry — first embodied for John's readers in Rome, whose certain judgment is celebrated.
Her smoke rises forever and ever

Echoes Isaiah 34:10, where Edom's smoke goes up forever, and the smoke of Sodom and Gomorrah rising like a furnace (Genesis 19:28). Edom and Sodom became stock types of irreversible judgment in prophetic and Second Temple literature.
Burned cities in antiquity smouldered for days; the sack of a city was signalled by its rising smoke (compare the burning of Rome in AD 64 and Jerusalem in AD 70).

The image stresses the finality of the judgment: the city will never be rebuilt. It mirrors the smoke of the worshippers' torment in 14:11 and contrasts with the smoke of incense from the saints' prayers in 8:4.
The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures… 'Amen, Hallelujah!'

'Amen. Hallelujah' is the closing doxology of Book IV of the Psalter (Psalm 106:48), and 'small and great' who fear the LORD comes from Psalm 115:13. The elders and living creatures recall the heavenly court of Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 and the priestly courses of 1 Chronicles 24-25.

The throne-room choir of chapters 4-5 reappears for the last time, sealing the hymn with 'Amen'. A voice from the throne then summons all God's servants, of every rank, to praise — the whole people of God join the heavenly court.
The Lord our God the Almighty reigns

Echoes the enthronement psalms ('The LORD reigns', Psalms 93:1, 96:10, 97:1, 99:1) and Isaiah 52:7. 'Almighty' (Greek pantokratōr) is the Septuagint's regular rendering of 'LORD of hosts' (YHWH Sabaoth), the divine warrior-king of Israel's armies.

Domitian is reported to have had himself styled 'our lord and god' (dominus et deus noster, Suetonius, Domitian 13), and emperors were hailed as kyrios. Revelation reserves 'Lord God Almighty' for Israel's God alone.

The aorist 'reigns' (or 'has begun to reign') celebrates God's kingship decisively displayed in judgment. It answers the seventh trumpet's announcement (11:15-17) and functions as a direct counter-claim to imperial titles.
The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready

The prophets cast the covenant as a marriage between YHWH and Israel (Hosea 2:16-20; Isaiah 54:5-6; 62:4-5; Jeremiah 2:2; Ezekiel 16:8-14), with a renewed wedding promised after exile. Jewish marriage proceeded in two stages: a binding betrothal (later called erusin), often a year in length, followed by the procession that brought the bride to the groom's home and a wedding feast that could last seven days (Genesis 29:27; Judges 14:12). Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20) and told parables of wedding feasts (Matthew 22:1-14; 25:1-13).

Greco-Roman weddings likewise centred on the bride's adornment and the torchlit procession to the husband's house followed by a banquet; the bride's preparation and dress were matters of public display.

The church, betrothed to Christ already (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25-27), now reaches the consummation of the covenant. The announcement anticipates the full description of the bride-city in 21:2, 9. 'Has come' is proleptic: it is announced here and described in chapters 21-22.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost) place the marriage in heaven between the rapture and the Second Coming, after the judgment seat of Christ; the marriage supper follows on earth, often linked with the opening of the millennium. The bride is the church, distinct from Israel and from the invited guests (OT and tribulation saints).

Chilton and others see the wedding as the public establishment of the new covenant bride once the adulterous old covenant 'wife' (apostate Jerusalem) has been divorced and judged in AD 70; the church now feasts with Christ, not least at the Lord's Supper, while awaiting final consummation.

Amillennial and idealist commentators (Beale, Hendriksen) read it as the consummated union of Christ and the whole people of God at the Second Coming, after a church age of betrothal; there is no separate stage between rapture and return.
Historicists such as Barnes saw the scene as the triumph and purity of the true church after the fall of papal Rome, ushering in a time of gospel ascendancy before the end.
Fine linen, bright and pure — the righteous acts of the saints

Fine linen (Hebrew shesh/bad) was the fabric of the tabernacle curtains and of priestly garments; on the Day of Atonement the high priest wore only white linen (Leviticus 16:4). Isaiah 61:10 pictures salvation as a bridegroom's and bride's wedding clothes. Daniel 12:10 speaks of the wise being purified and made white.

Linen, especially Egyptian byssus, was a luxury textile; the same word appears among Babylon's cargo (18:12) and her clothing (18:16). The bride's linen is a pointed contrast with the prostitute's purple and scarlet.

The bride's dress is 'given' to her (divine gift) and yet consists of the saints' righteous deeds (plural dikaiōmata): grace and faithful obedience together. Some commentators read the deeds as God's vindicating verdicts for the saints; most take them as the saints' faithful witness. The priestly colour fits a bride who is also a kingdom of priests.
Blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb

Isaiah 25:6-8 promises a banquet for all peoples on Mount Zion when God swallows up death. Second Temple texts develop this messianic banquet: 1 Enoch 62:14 (the righteous eat with the Son of Man forever); 2 Baruch 29:4-8 (Behemoth and Leviathan become food for the survivors, manna falls again); the Qumran Rule of the Congregation (1QSa 2:11-22) describes a meal at which the Messiah of Israel sits. Jesus spoke of many coming from east and west to recline with Abraham (Matthew 8:11) and of drinking new wine in the kingdom (Matthew 26:29).
Banquets were central to patronage in the Roman world; an invitation signalled honour and belonging, and seating reflected status. Trade-guild banquets often involved idol meat (Revelation 2:14, 20).

The fourth of Revelation's seven beatitudes. The Lamb's banquet is the opposite of the 'great supper of God' in 19:17: one is a feast of fellowship, the other a feast of carrion. Whether the guests are the same as the bride (most commentators: yes, a mixed metaphor) or a distinct group (dispensational reading) is debated.
Pentecost and Walvoord distinguish the bride (the church) from the guests (Old Testament and tribulation saints), and many place the supper on earth at the start of the millennial kingdom.
Amillennialists usually treat bride and guests as two images of the one people of God and locate the supper at the consummation, foreshadowed in the Lord's Supper.
Some partial preterists stress that the church already sits at the Lamb's table in the eucharist since the new covenant was fully established, while still expecting its fullness at the end.
Do not do that… Worship God! The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy

Jewish monotheism forbade worship of angels; the angel's refusal parallels the angel Raphael in Tobit 12:16-22 and the angel in the Ascension of Isaiah (7:21; 8:5) who refuses worship. Colossians 2:18 warns against the 'worship of angels', reflecting angel veneration on the fringes of Judaism in Asia Minor.
Inscriptions from Asia Minor (e.g. around Colossae and Laodicea) attest local veneration of angels; the region was fertile ground for confusion over intermediary beings.

Even the greatest revealing angel is a 'fellow servant'; worship belongs to God alone — which makes the worship of the Lamb in chapter 5 so significant. 'Testimony of Jesus' may be objective (testimony about Jesus) or subjective (the testimony Jesus himself gave); either way, true prophecy is Christ-centred witness, and all who bear it share the prophetic Spirit. The scene is repeated almost verbatim in 22:8-9.
I saw heaven standing open

Ezekiel's visions begin with the heavens opened (Ezekiel 1:1); Isaiah prays that God would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). In 3 Maccabees 6:18 heaven's gates open and angels descend to rescue Jews. At Jesus' baptism the heavens are torn open (Mark 1:10).

Earlier a door was opened in heaven (4:1) and the heavenly temple opened (11:19; 15:5); now heaven itself stands open for the divine warrior to come out. The image signals a climactic revelation and intervention.
A white horse, and its rider is called Faithful and True

Zechariah's visions include angelic horsemen (Zechariah 1:8; 6:1-8). 2 Maccabees reports heavenly horsemen in shining armour fighting for Israel (2 Maccabees 3:25; 5:2-3; 10:29-30). The divine warrior who 'judges in righteousness' recalls Isaiah 11:4-5 and Psalm 96:13. 'Faithful and True' repeats Christ's title to Laodicea (3:14), itself echoing the 'God of Amen' (Isaiah 65:16).

A Roman general celebrating a triumph rode in a chariot drawn by white horses, followed by his army and captives; white horses were also associated with Persian and Parthian royalty. The image presents Christ's victory as the true triumph.

Almost all interpreters identify the rider as Christ (contrast the rider of 6:2, whose identity is disputed). The scene gathers Old Testament warrior imagery around Jesus and pictures his decisive victory over the beast, the false prophet and their allies. What event it portrays is the key disagreement.

Futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) see the visible, bodily Second Coming of Christ at the end of the seven-year tribulation, defeating the Antichrist's armies at Armageddon and then establishing the millennial kingdom described in chapter 20.

Amillennialists and idealists (Hendriksen, Beale, Riddlebarger) also see the Second Coming, but as the end of one of several parallel cycles; chapter 20 then steps back to the beginning of the church age rather than following chronologically.

Many partial preterists and postmillennialists (Chilton) read 19:11-21 as Christ's ongoing conquest of the nations through the gospel — the 'sword of his mouth' — from his ascension and the judgment of AD 70 onward; others in the school take it as the final Second Coming.

Historicists commonly read it as the final, perhaps still future, triumph of Christ over papal and anti-Christian powers, either by his personal return or by a mighty spread of the gospel (Barnes favoured the latter).

Full preterists (Russell, Preston) identify it with Christ's coming in judgment in AD 70, which they hold was the one Second Coming; critics note this denies the future bodily return confessed in the creeds, while proponents reply that the same 'soon' governs this coming as the rest of the book (22:6-7, 12).
Eyes like blazing fire
Daniel's heavenly man has eyes 'like flaming torches' (Daniel 10:6). In 1 Enoch 106:5-6 the newborn Noah's eyes blaze like the sun, a sign of heavenly origin.
Repeats the description of Christ in 1:14 and to Thyatira (2:18): penetrating, all-seeing judgment. The rider is the same Lord who walked among the lampstands.
Many royal crowns (diadems) on His head

1 Maccabees 11:13 records Ptolemy VI entering Antioch and putting on two diadems, those of Asia and of Egypt, to claim both kingdoms. Psalm 21:3 and Zechariah 6:11 picture crowns for the messianic king-priest.
The diadēma was a cloth band of Hellenistic royalty, symbolising sovereign rule (distinct from the stephanos, the victor's wreath). Multiple diadems signalled rule over several realms.
The dragon wears seven diadems (12:3) and the beast ten (13:1); Christ wears 'many', outnumbering every rival claim. His sovereignty is universal and genuine where theirs is usurped.
A name written on Him that only He Himself knows

When Jacob and Manoah ask the divine messenger's name, it is withheld as 'wonderful' (Genesis 32:29; Judges 13:18). Isaiah 62:2 promises a new name for Zion. In Jewish tradition the divine name was not pronounced aloud except by the high priest on the Day of Atonement.
Greco-Roman magical papyri sought to control spirits by knowing their secret names. Christ's name cannot be manipulated.

The hidden name marks Christ's divine transcendence and freedom: no one controls him. Yet three names are also disclosed — Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings — revelation and mystery together. It may also connect to the new name promised to the overcomer (2:17; 3:12).
A robe dipped in blood

Isaiah 63:1-6 pictures YHWH returning from Edom and Bozrah with garments red from treading the winepress, spattered with the blood of the nations. Genesis 49:11 (Judah washing his garments in the blood of grapes) was read messianically: the Palestinian Targums (Neofiti, Pseudo-Jonathan — of uncertain and probably later date) depict the king-messiah girding for battle and reddening the mountains with the blood of the slain.

The blood is stained before the battle begins (19:19), which leads many to see it as Christ's own blood (5:9; 7:14) or the martyrs' blood that he avenges, reinterpreting Isaiah 63: the warrior conquers as the slain Lamb. Others read it straightforwardly as the enemies' blood as in Isaiah. Both may be in view.
His name is The Word of God

The Wisdom of Solomon 18:14-16 describes God's all-powerful word leaping from heaven's royal throne on Passover night as a stern warrior carrying a sharp sword, filling Egypt with death. God's word goes out and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11); by it the heavens were made (Psalm 33:6).
Stoic philosophy spoke of the Logos as the rational principle governing the cosmos; John's Logos is personal and acts in judgment.

The title links Revelation with the Johannine Prologue (John 1:1, 14) and presents Christ as God's decisive self-expression whose spoken word judges. In context it explains the sword from his mouth: he conquers by his word of truth.
The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him on white horses

The LORD comes 'with all his holy ones' (Zechariah 14:5; Deuteronomy 33:2), and 1 Enoch 1:9 (quoted in Jude 14-15) pictures him coming with myriads of holy ones to judge. The Qumran War Scroll (1QM) imagines angels fighting alongside the sons of light in the final war.
In a Roman triumph the victorious army marched behind the general; here the army carries no weapons.

The fine linen links the armies with the bride (19:8), and 17:14 says those with the Lamb are 'called, chosen and faithful', suggesting the saints; angelic armies (Matthew 25:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7) are also likely included. Notably the army does no fighting — the victory belongs to the rider's word.
Dispensationalists see the raptured, glorified church (plus angels) returning with Christ after the marriage in heaven — evidence, they argue, that the rapture preceded this event.
Amillennial and many other commentators see angels and the saints (as in 17:14) accompanying Christ at his single return, without implying a prior separate rapture.
From His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations

The shoot of Jesse strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth and slays the wicked with the breath of his lips (Isaiah 11:4); the Servant's mouth is made like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2). Psalms of Solomon 17:24, 35 has the Davidic Messiah destroy lawless nations by the word of his mouth; in 4 Ezra 13:9-11 the man from the sea annihilates the hostile multitude with a stream of fire from his mouth.
The Roman short sword (gladius) and the right to execute (ius gladii) symbolised imperial power held by provincial governors.

Christ's weapon is his word — of truth, judgment and gospel. It echoes 1:16 and the warning to Pergamum (2:16). The image deliberately avoids a literal battle: no fighting is described, only a verdict spoken and executed.
Postmillennialists (Chilton, Gentry) stress that the sword is the gospel word by which Christ subdues the nations through history — the Great Commission is the means of this conquest.
Futurists hold that Christ's spoken word will literally and instantly destroy the armies gathered against him at his return, as 2 Thessalonians 2:8 also describes.
Idealists see the decisive power of Christ's truth and judgment over every opposing power, finally displayed at the end.
He will rule them with an iron scepter

Psalm 2:9, a royal coronation psalm: the Davidic son will shepherd/break the nations with a rod of iron. The Septuagint reads 'shepherd' (poimainō) rather than 'break'. Psalms of Solomon 17:23-24 applies the same verse to the Messiah smashing sinners' arrogance like a potter's jar.

The third use of Psalm 2:9 in Revelation (2:27; 12:5): the messianic son's authority is now exercised. The verb blends shepherding and shattering — rule that protects the flock and destroys its enemies.
Premillennialists see a literal reign of Christ over nations during the millennium, when some still need firm rule (compare 20:7-9).
Amillennialists see the present heavenly reign of the enthroned Son (Psalm 2:6-8; Acts 13:33) culminating in final judgment.
He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty

Isaiah 63:3 (the warrior who tramples the winepress alone) and Joel 3:13 (the winepress is full, for their wickedness is great); Lamentations 1:15 uses the image of the Lord treading Judah as in a winepress.
Grapes were trodden by foot in stone vats; the red juice running out made a vivid picture of bloodshed, familiar in the vine-growing regions of Asia Minor.
Picks up the harvest-judgment of 14:17-20 and assigns the treading to Christ himself. The piling up of terms ('fury of the wrath') stresses the full measure of God's judgment.
A name written on His robe and on His thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS

God is 'God of gods and Lord of lords' (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 136:2-3); 'King of kings' is used of God in 1 Enoch 9:4 and 2 Maccabees 13:4, and of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2:37 (Daniel 4:37 in the Greek reads 'God of gods and Lord of lords and King of kings'). The thigh was where a sword was worn (Psalm 45:3) and where oaths were sworn (Genesis 24:2).

'King of kings' was a title of Persian and Parthian monarchs, Rome's eastern rivals. Ancient writers mention statues with inscriptions on the thigh — Cicero describes a statue of Apollo with the sculptor Myron's name in small silver letters on its thigh (Against Verres 2.4.93).
The title reverses the beast's claim (17:14 already gave it to the Lamb). Placed where a warrior's sword would hang and visible as he rides, it declares Christ's supremacy over every earthly ruler.
An angel standing in the sun… 'Come, gather together for the great supper of God'

Ezekiel 39:17-20 summons birds and beasts to a sacrificial feast on the flesh of Gog's warriors, horses and riders. Leaving bodies unburied for birds was a covenant curse (Deuteronomy 28:26; Jeremiah 7:33) and a central horror in Jewish piety (Tobit 1-2).
Denial of burial was the ultimate disgrace in both Jewish and Greco-Roman culture (Antigone's dilemma; Roman practice of leaving crucified bodies to scavengers).

A dark parody of the marriage supper: those who refuse the Lamb's banquet become the meal. The list from kings to slaves (echoing 6:15) shows judgment without respect to rank. The angel's position in the sun gives him a vantage point to summon all the birds in mid-heaven (8:13; 14:6).
Futurists see literal carnage after the Battle of Armageddon at Christ's return.

Idealists and many amillennialists read the imagery as the total and shameful defeat of the enemies of God at the final judgment, drawn from Ezekiel's Gog oracle; the same battle is retold in 20:7-10.
Chilton linked the imagery to the slaughter that followed the fall of Jerusalem and the defeat of Christ's first-century enemies; other partial preterists read it of the final judgment.
The beast and the kings of the earth with their armies assembled to wage war
Psalm 2:2: the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed. Joel 3:2, 9-14 and Zechariah 14:2 gather the nations for judgment; Ezekiel 38-39 gathers Gog's hordes.
Client kings allied to Rome supplied auxiliary troops; the 'kings of the east' recall the Parthian threat (16:12).

This is the gathering prepared in 16:12-16 (Armageddon) and anticipated in 17:14; the Greek speaks of 'the war', a definite, known conflict. Many commentators argue that 20:8 describes the same war with the same Ezekiel 38-39 imagery.

Amillennialists (Beale, White) argue that 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 all use the article — 'the war' — and all draw on Ezekiel 38-39, so they describe one final battle viewed from different angles (recapitulation).
Historic premillennialists (Ladd) and dispensationalists see two battles: Armageddon at Christ's return (19:19) and a later Gog-Magog revolt after the millennium (20:8).
The beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur

Daniel 7:11: the fourth beast is slain and its body given to the burning fire. Korah's rebels went down 'alive' into Sheol (Numbers 16:33). Fire and sulfur rained on Sodom (Genesis 19:24); Isaiah 30:33 describes the burning pit (Topheth) kindled by the breath of the LORD. 1 Enoch 90:24-26 sees the fallen stars and blind sheep thrown into a fiery abyss.

Asia Minor was volcanic and sulfurous; the hot springs of Hierapolis near Laodicea and its 'Plutonium' (a cave emitting deadly vapours believed to be an entrance to the underworld) gave vivid local images of a fiery underworld.

The first inhabitants of the lake of fire are the two beasts of chapter 13 — the persecuting state power and its propaganda-priesthood. 'Alive' stresses a summary, conscious judgment. The devil follows in 20:10.

Partial preterists commonly identify the beast with Nero/Rome and the false prophet with the imperial cult priesthood or the Jewish leaders who enforced it; their 'capture' is their historic overthrow (Nero's suicide in AD 68, the fall of Jerusalem).
Historicists identify the beast and false prophet with the papal civil-ecclesiastical system and its spiritual authority, whose final overthrow is still awaited or partially accomplished.
Futurists see two individuals — the Antichrist and his religious promoter — personally cast into the lake of fire at Christ's return, a thousand years before Satan joins them (20:10).
Idealists see the end of the recurring powers of persecuting state and deceptive religion, decisively judged at the consummation.
Signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image

Deuteronomy 13:1-5 warns of prophets whose signs come true but who lead to other gods; Pharaoh's magicians imitated Moses' signs (Exodus 7:11-12). Daniel 3 tells of the image all must worship on pain of death.

The imperial cult used statues of the emperor, priesthoods, festivals and sometimes staged wonders; participation was bound up with civic and guild life (Pergamum, Smyrna, Ephesus all had imperial temples).
A summary recalling chapter 13: the deceivers and the deceived share the same fate. The sentence underlines that deception is culpable allegiance, not innocent mistake.
The rest were killed with the sword… all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh
Fulfils the summons of Ezekiel 39:17-20 and the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:26.

The followers of the beast fall by the word of Christ rather than by human armies; the vision ends in total victory. Whether this means the death of all the unbelieving on earth (raising the question of who populates the millennium in 20:3, 8) is debated.

Amillennialists note that if all enemies are killed here, the 'nations' deceived again in 20:8 must refer to the same final conflict viewed afresh — evidence against strict chronological sequence from 19 to 20.

Dispensationalists answer that 19:21 describes the armies gathered at Armageddon, not every person; survivors who enter the millennium in natural bodies (Matthew 25:31-46) produce the nations deceived at its end.

For partial preterists such as Chilton and Gentry, chapter 19 celebrates the definitive judgment of the persecuting order (often apostate Jerusalem as the prostitute, with Rome as the beast) and the vindication of the new covenant church as Christ's bride. Many read the rider as Christ's ongoing victory through the gospel after AD 70, with the beast's downfall fulfilled in the collapse of Nero and the first-century persecutors; others in the school take 19:11-21 as the future Second Coming.

Full preterists (Russell, King, Preston) see the marriage, the rider's appearing and the lake of fire as fulfilled together in AD 70, which they regard as the one Second Coming. Critics from every other school object that this leaves no future bodily return or resurrection, contrary to the historic creeds; proponents reply that the New Testament's time texts require it and that the 'coming' was covenantal and spiritual.

Historicists (Elliott, Barnes) read the chapter as the overthrow of papal Rome and the anti-Christian powers, still future or underway in their day, followed by the triumph of true Christianity; many expected the rider's victory to come through a worldwide spread of the gospel preceding the millennium.

Futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) take the chapter as the climax of the seven-year tribulation: the marriage of the Lamb in heaven, then Christ's visible, bodily return with his saints to defeat the Antichrist and false prophet at Armageddon, immediately followed by the millennial kingdom of chapter 20. They argue that the narrative sequence (heaven opened, the beast seized, then the angel binding Satan) and the close parallels to Matthew 24:30, Acts 1:11 and 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8 and 2:8 make this the clearest picture in Scripture of a personal, visible return in glory.

Idealists (Hendriksen, in part Beale) see the final scene of one of Revelation's parallel cycles: the consummation of Christ's victory over the beast-power and false religion that oppose the church in every age, culminating in his return. Chapter 20 then restarts the story from the first coming.

Eclectic interpreters (Osborne, Keener, Mounce) generally read 19:11-21 as the future Second Coming portrayed through Old Testament holy-war imagery, while recognising the first-century Roman target of the beast language and a symbolic rather than literal battle.

Dispensational premillennialists insist that 19:11-20:6 is a chronological sequence: the Second Coming (19:11) precedes the binding of Satan and the thousand-year reign (20:1-6), so the millennium must follow Christ's return.

Historic premillennialists (Ladd, Mounce) agree that 19 to 20 reads naturally as a sequence — Christ returns, then Satan is bound — but without a pre-tribulation rapture or the dispensational Israel/church distinction.

Amillennialists (Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Beale) argue that 20:1 begins a new vision (signalled by 'Then I saw') that recapitulates the church age, because the same Ezekiel 38-39 battle appears in 19:17-21 and 20:8-10, and because the nations are destroyed in 19 yet present in 20.

Postmillennialists divide: some (Chilton) read 19:11-21 as the gospel conquest of the nations, which then issues in the millennial era of 20; others (Warfield) read it as a symbolic picture of the whole victorious gospel age, the 'binding' and 'reign' of chapter 20 describing the same period from heaven's side.
Why might heaven's 'Hallelujah' be celebrated over an act of judgment? How does Revelation keep that from becoming vindictiveness?
The rider's robe is bloodied before the battle begins and his only weapon comes from his mouth. What does that suggest about how Christ conquers?
Compare the two suppers of chapter 19. What does each reveal about the choice set before the readers?
Does 20:1 follow 19:21 in time, or begin a new vision? List the textual clues each side uses.
How would believers in the imperial cities of Asia have heard titles like 'Lord God Almighty' and 'King of kings'?
The Binding of Satan, the Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
The millennium and the final judgment (20:1-15)

An angel with the key of the Abyss seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals him in the Abyss so that he can no longer deceive the nations. John sees thrones and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, who 'came to life' and reigned with Christ for the thousand years — the 'first resurrection', over which the second death has no power. After the thousand years Satan is released, gathers Gog and Magog from the four corners of the earth against the camp of the saints and the beloved city, and is destroyed by fire from heaven and thrown into the lake of fire. Finally the dead, great and small, stand before a great white throne, books are opened, all are judged by their deeds, and Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire. This short passage — the only place Scripture mentions a thousand-year reign — is the storm-centre of Christian eschatology, generating the postmillennial, amillennial and premillennial positions.
